rv.q: In the end, Di and Viv and Rose is a moving and surprising pleasure of an evening, that sends you out into the night with a lump in your throat.
Bullmore hits all the targets Souter aims at, and more.
Bullmore’s play wittily explores its ongoing consolations.

It doesn’t feel quite so organic here and the production really misses McKee’s prickly, complex take on the character of Viv. Spiro’s Viv is broader, less of a puzzle, and now it’s Outhwaite’s Di who feels the more nuanced of three. It’s also easier to see the emotional machinery of the play at work this time around.
Peter Barnes' exuberant play, which, amazingly, has not had a major revival since its 1968 premiere, fizzes with comedy, ideas and dramatic invention.

Nevertheless, the trio do a decent job of fleshing them out; their portrayal of youthful exuberance, first love and cider-drinking from cereal bowls is no less playful played by women in their 40s than actresses in their teens. When the time comes for them to leave university – and each other – the separation is authentically painful.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this warm, funny exploration of female friendship, with strong performances winning most over. One dissenter finds it too slight for the West End, but the consensus applauds Bullmore's tender, comic writing.
